articles.title: Armenia's exports to Russia raise concerns over sanctions circumvention - rapporteur.com
articles.summary: Armenia's exports to Russia raise concerns over sanctions circumvention  rapporteur.com
articles.full_text:
Despite deteriorating political relations between Armenia and Russia, bilateral trade has flourished, leaving Western partners wondering over Yerevan’s approach to sanctions.
In the aftermath of the sanctions against Moscow, Armenia’s exports to Russia tripled in 2022 and then doubled between January and August 2023, providing ground for accusations about the South Caucasus country’s compliance with the Western sanctions regime.
While the political relations of Armenia with Russia have largely deteriorated in the last few years, bilateral trade with Russia flourished.
Risky trade partner
Since Armenia’s accession in 2014 to the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union, Russia has become Armenia’s number one trading partner. Russia’s share in foreign exports of Armenia further increased in the aftermath of the invasion of Ukraine.
In 2023, trade with Russia accounted for over 35% of the country’s foreign trade, compared with the EU’s 13% share in the total.
The Armenian economy’s high dependency on its trade with Russia has made it practically impossible for the country to join the sanctions against Moscow without risking unprecedented economic downfall.
This growing economic dependency on the Russian market does not, however, impede the Armenian government’s attempts to slowly shift the country’s geopolitical orientation towards the West.
Quite the contrary, the tensions between the Kremlin and Yerevan, including Armenia’s open disagreement with the Kremlin’s war of aggression, continue to grow in parallel with the increase of trade numbers.
Many in Armenia are worried that the Kremlin can use Armenia’s economic dependency as political leverage, with recent opinion polls conducted by the International Republican Institute (IRI) showing that 40% of Armenians view Russia as the most significant political threat to their country, after Turkey and Azerbaijan.
Meanwhile, Russia has in recent months already blocked on several occasions the import of Armenian products on its ground checkpoint with Georgia.
Increase in re-exports
In 2022, the volume of trade between Armenia and Russia nearly doubled, reaching $5.3 billion, according to Armenia’s state statistics agency. This trend continued apace in 2023 and in the early months of 2024. The increase in Armenia’s exports to Russia is largely due to the re-export of products from third countries.
According to the UN Comtrade Database, the list of products exported from Armenia to Russia in the last two years includes but is not limited to, mobile phones, computers, headphones, and other technical equipment.
In recent months the re-export of diamonds and gold has also been on the rise.
To avoid possible issues with compliance with the sanctions regime, the Armenian government has made the data on trade with Russia publicly available and has invested in providing almost real-time updates on imports and exports to the Russian Federation.
“There is a rise in re-exports, the products being re-exported are not currently under sanctions, or at least not yet,” Seda Hergnyan of Hetq.am Investigative platform, specialising in monitoring Armenia’s compliance with sanctions, told Euractiv.
“However, if tomorrow the collective West decides to consider the re-exports to Russia as sanctions circumvention, all of Armenia’s exports will be put at risk, but the primary risks associated with increased re-exports are risks for Armenia’s economic development itself,” Hergnyan said
“There are growing concerns that Armenia’s economic growth rate is becoming even more dependent on the Russian market. This economic growth process is not stable and is reliant on external factors rather than internal economic development and increased production rates. These external factors can change overnight,” she cautioned.
For now, however, according to Hergnyan, the re-export process is transparent and is openly documented by Armenia’s public statistics service.
She is not the sole journalist in Armenia who agrees that the data is transparent and updated almost in real-time. This transparency is supposedly helping the Armenian government to dispel doubts regarding its intentions.
Meanwhile, to increase oversight of possible sanctions circumvention by Armenia-registered companies, the country’s authorities introduced in 2023 mandatory government licenses for shipments of microchips, transformers, video cameras, antennas, and other electronic equipment to Russia.
A contradiction of views
Since February 2022, the increased export figures are occasionally presented in Western media as proof that Armenia is deliberately helping Russia circumvent the sanctions regime.
“We regularly see waves of English language posts on X, often initiated by Azerbaijani users, that accuse Armenia of deliberately helping Russia to circumvent the sanctions,” Ani Grigoryan, the editor and founder of #CivilNetCheck, told Euractiv.
In addition, she said, some foreign experts, genuinely concerned with the compliance of third parties with sanctions against Russia, also sometimes present data on Armenia’s trade with Russia as proof of non-compliance.
“The numbers are often presented without any context or with no reference to the particularities or vulnerabilities of Armenia’s context. Even if the numbers are not fake, their representation without relevant context analysis can become a manipulation,” she said.
The accusations of Armenia’s sanctions circumvention have recently been addressed even by Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan. In an interview with France 24, he stressed that neither the European Union nor the United States have any reservations regarding Armenia’s compliance with sanctions.
The US and EU officials have indeed stated on several occasions that Armenia’s authorities are cooperating with Western partners.
During a US House of Representatives Foreign Affairs Committee’s hearing in November, Assistant State Secretary James O’Brien praised the reforms undertaken by the Armenian government that allow the US administration to track the trade with Russia.
“In almost real-time, they can see which firms are involved in this circumvention trade, and then we’re able to take measures to stop that trade. It works remarkably well,” he stated.
In March 2024, the European Parliament assessed positively Armenia’s overall record of cooperation in the context of sanctions.
In its resolution on closer ties between the EU and Armenia, the European Parliament noted that despite the increased exports to Russia the EU’s Special Envoy on Sanctions, David O’Sullivan, has not voiced any concern over Armenian authorities’ cooperation with the EU on preventing sanctions circumvention.
“There appears to be a divergence of opinions between the Western expert community and officials from the US and EU on this matter,” Hovhannes Nazaretyan of EVN Report, a prominent Armenian analytical media platform, told Euractiv.
“While some experts occasionally accuse Armenia of attempting to circumvent sanctions, officials from both Brussels and Washington commend Armenia for its transparency in providing information and for its compliance with the requirements of the sanctions regime,” Nazaretyan told Euractiv.
However, despite the positive statements of relevant EU and US bodies specialised in monitoring sanctions implementation, Armenian experts stress the need to monitor both the Armenian government’s policies on sanctions and the media manipulation waves on English language media platforms.

articles.title: Rosneft - A7 - 2Rivers: How Oil Revenues Became a Financial Infrastructure for Sanctions Evasion - Robert Lansing Institute
articles.summary: Rosneft - A7 - 2Rivers: How Oil Revenues Became a Financial Infrastructure for Sanctions Evasion  Robert Lansing Institute
articles.full_text:
The leak of A7’s internal documents reveals the emergence of a parallel mechanism for international settlements in which export revenues from Russian oil provided the foreign-currency liquidity needed to pay for imports into Russia, including military and dual-use goods.
The key lies in the connection among three elements: Rosneft as the generator of export revenues; Coral Energy/2Rivers as the external trading interface; and A7 as the clearing and payments infrastructure that allowed those revenues to be converted into payments to foreign suppliers.
Key Findings
Documents obtained by the Financial Times indicate that A7 moved at least $6.9 billion through the international banking system between late 2024 and August 2025. The FT identified around 100 companies that actually executed payments and references to roughly another 100 entities in internal documents. The network extended across the UAE, Hong Kong, Kyrgyzstan, Indonesia and European jurisdictions.
Rosneft was not fully blocked by OFAC during the period covered by the leak. The United States imposed blocking sanctions on the company itself only on October 22, 2025, although restrictions affecting Rosneft and Russia’s energy sector had existed in various forms since 2014. It is therefore more accurate to describe the arrangement as a mechanism for monetizing Russian oil revenues under sanctions and restrictions on the Russian oil sector, rather than to suggest that every transaction described by the FT constituted payment for oil from an already OFAC-blocked Rosneft.
By contrast, the intermediary 2Rivers – formerly Coral Energy – was placed under British sanctions on December 17, 2024. British authorities explicitly described 2Rivers as one of the key intermediaries in Russian oil trading. The EU later concluded that 2Rivers facilitated exports of Russian oil, including Rosneft oil, concealed its actual origin and controlled a significant share of vessels in Russia’s “shadow fleet.”
How the Oil-Revenue Collection and Use Scheme Worked
Based on the FT documents, the mechanism can be reconstructed approximately as follows: Rosneft → traders/affiliated companies → foreign oil buyer → dirhams/yuan → A7 offshore company → international bank/SWIFT → foreign supplier → goods → Russia.
At the same time, a second, ruble-denominated leg of the settlement could operate inside Russia: Russian importer → rubles → A7/Russian financial circuit.
The foreign currency did not necessarily have to return physically to Russia. It could remain in the UAE, China, Hong Kong or another jurisdiction and be used to meet the external obligations of Russian clients.
In this way, oil exports were transformed into a kind of offshore liquidity pool.
Stage 1. Oil Sales
The principal external trader mentioned in the documents was Coral Energy, later renamed 2Rivers. According to the FT materials, A7 received foreign currency from 16 companies linked to Rosneft, most of which were also connected to Coral. One A7 employee explicitly described Coral as Rosneft’s trader “from which we receive yuan.”
This is consistent with the EU’s later assessment: its sanctions decision on 2Rivers explicitly states that the group facilitated the supply and export of Russian oil, particularly Rosneft oil, and concealed its true origin.
The trader therefore functioned as a buffer between the Russian producer and the international buyer.
Formally, A7 is headed by Ilan Shor, the Moldovan businessman based in Russia. As of 2026, Reuters identifies him as A7’s CEO; he publicly represents the company and its international expansion.
The control structure, however, is broader:
- Ilan Shor – co-founder, CEO and key public figure. A7’s initial ownership structure was 51% Shor / 49% PSB (Promsvyazbank). Shor is also listed as chief executive of the subsidiary A7 Agent. Promsvyazbank is a Russian state-owned bank focused on servicing the defense sector. OFAC explicitly states that A7 and its subsidiaries are owned by Shor and Promsvyazbank.
- Petr Fradkov, head of PSB, plays an important institutional role in the system. In August 2026, he said that A7 served about 15,000 regular business clients and processed up to 2,000 cross-border payments a day. VEB.RF also appears in A7’s financial architecture: PSB’s stake was pledged to VEB.RF as collateral for A7 loans. This points to the involvement of another state financial institution. A7’s internal materials obtained by the FT mention senior executive Stanislav Lazarev. According to the documents, it was Lazarev who discussed with colleagues the possibility of receiving from Rosneft the equivalent of roughly $12 billion in yuan. The FT describes A7 as Shor’s structure, created with the support of the state-owned PSB.
Stanislav Lazarev is one of A7’s key operational executives, responsible for corporate business/sales and cross-border settlements. A7 internal documents obtained by the FT show his involvement in discussions about a large source of yuan liquidity from Rosneft. Open professional databases contain a profile of a Moscow banker with the same name and experience at Raiffeisenbank, but the identity of that individual as the A7 executive has not been independently confirmed.
An investigation by Proekt alleged that Roman Abramovich and businessman Viktor Kharitonin may have links to A7. A source for the outlet described Abramovich as A7’s “protector and sponsor,” while companies associated with Kharitonin allegedly provided A7 with multibillion-ruble loans. Abramovich’s representative categorically denied any connection, ownership stake or involvement in arrangements concerning A7. The allegation should therefore be treated as an unconfirmed version rather than an established fact.
A7 is difficult to regard as an ordinary private business belonging to Shor: 49% is owned by the state-controlled PSB, financing/collateral involving VEB.RF is present, and the infrastructure itself is closely tied to PSB. OFAC explicitly characterizes A7 as a Russian cross-border settlement platform used to evade sanctions.
According to open-source information, Ilan Shor’s intelligence-service connection is far better documented with the FSB. Much of the evidence concerns the FSB’s Fifth Service -the Service for Operational Information and International Relations – which traditionally operates across the post-Soviet space. A Washington Post investigation based on intercepted materials and information from Ukrainian, Moldovan and Western sources described Shor as an important component of FSB operations in Moldova. According to the newspaper, FSB documents referred to him as “the young one.” The FSB directed substantial funds toward a network of Moldovan politicians and influence operations in which Shor played a central role.
This is consistent with later information from Moldova’s SIS. The service said that an operational command center had been established in Moscow to interfere in Moldova’s elections and referendum, and that the Russian side designated Shor to lead the relevant network, providing it with financial, media, personnel, logistical and technical resources as well as counterintelligence support.
The last detail is particularly significant. Providing counterintelligence support to a political network abroad fits the FSB’s profile more closely than an ordinary Kremlin relationship with a political ally.
The working model is: Kremlin → FSB/Fifth Service → Shor → political, financial and influence networks in Moldova.
After Shor moved to Russia, his role appears to have expanded. He is no longer merely an operator on the Moldovan track. Through A7, Shor became embedded in a much larger state-linked financial infrastructure. A7 was created with the participation of the state defense bank PSB and is now one of the major operators of Russian cross-border payments. Reuters identified Shor as A7’s CEO in June 2026.
Ilan Shor is a Russian proxy and financial-political operator whose best-documented intelligence-service connection leads to the FSB and its operational infrastructure in the post-Soviet space.
The key question is whether, after the creation of A7, Shor remained an asset/operator of the FSB’s Fifth Service or whether his financial infrastructure came under broader interagency Kremlin control involving PSB, the FSB, the Presidential Administration and other security services.
The Most Important Resource Is Not Oil, but Foreign Currency
After 2022, Moscow faced a specific problem: Russia could continue selling enormous volumes of raw materials, but using the foreign currency earned from those sales became more difficult because of sanctions on banks, restrictions on correspondent accounts and scrutiny of international payments.
A7 effectively addressed the spatial disconnect between exports and imports.
For example: a buyer of Russian oil pays not a Russian bank but an intermediary company in the UAE → the foreign currency does not return to Russia → A7 uses it to pay a Chinese supplier → the Russian buyer of the goods settles with A7 in rubles inside Russia.
As a result, a direct international payment from Russia to China may never take place.
Instead, two internally balanced flows effectively occur: oil buyer → offshore pool → Chinese supplier, and Russian importer → A7 → Russian financial circuit.
This resembles multilateral clearing, but organized through a network of nominally independent legal entities.
Why Rosneft May Have Been Critical to A7
Every parallel payment system faces a fundamental problem: where can it obtain a steady supply of hard currency?
Russian importers need yuan, dirhams, dollars and euros to make purchases abroad. Oil companies, by contrast, continuously generate precisely those currencies.
The two flows naturally complement one another.

articles.title: French national released from Azerbaijani jail after EU drops sanctions on Russian oligarchs - OC Media
articles.summary: French national released from Azerbaijani jail after EU drops sanctions on Russian oligarchs  OC Media
articles.full_text:
The EU has struck a deal to delist two Russian oligarchs, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, in order to renew the larger bloc-wide sanctions for another year. The day after the deal was struck — apparently part of the agreement — Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed a pardon order for French citizen Martin Ryan, who was serving a 10-year prison sentence on espionage charges.
A number of countries, particularly the Baltic states and Ukraine, strongly protested the decision to delist Usmanov and Fridman.
Earlier in September, the Financial Times reported, citing sources, that France had been lobbying to have Usmanov delisted from the sanctions list in exchange for Azerbaijan releasing French nationals imprisoned in the country. For their part, Baku denied it had been lobbying France to delist Usmanov.
It is unclear why Azerbaijan was so keen on having Usmanov, a dual citizen of Russia and Uzbekistan with few apparent connections to Azerbaijan, removed from the sanctions list. There has been widespread speculation that Baku may have obtained something else from the deal, particularly from Russia or Uzbekistan, but there has been no official confirmation of what kind of quid pro quo exchange may have transpired.
The secretive nature of the deal raised further eyebrows in light of the strained relationship between Russia and Azerbaijan since Russian anti-air missiles mistakenly targeted an Azerbaijan Airlines passenger jet in December 2024, causing it to crash and killing 38 people on board.
A further dimension of the geopolitical drama concerns the long-standing friction between France and Azerbaijan, which largely stems from French support for Armenia.
In addition to Ryan, another French national, water executive Anass Derraz, is imprisoned in Azerbaijan.
In November 2025, Derraz was sentenced to 12 years in prison on charges of accepting bribes from Russian–Azerbaijani billionaire Farkhad Akhmedov. His sentence was reduced to nine years in June.
It does not appear that Derrazz was also released as part of the deal, and Azerbaijan has not specified the names of the other four foreigners who were pardoned alongside Ryan.
The Azerbaijani government has previously denied allegations that they have arrested foreign citizens for political reasons, while French authorities have raised concern. On 17 September, France’s Foreign Affairs Ministry issued a travel advisory warning French citizens about the risk of ‘arbitrary detention and unfair trials’ in Azerbaijan.
Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Aykhan Hajizada criticised the advisory the following day.
‘We call on the French side to refrain from unfounded and biased claims about Azerbaijan, respect our country’s sovereignty and internal affairs, and put an end to approaches that harm bilateral relations,’ Hajizada said.

articles.title: Trump wants potash from Belarus. A Canadian premier warns it would have to go through Russia. - Business Insider
articles.summary: Trump wants potash from Belarus. A Canadian premier warns it would have to go through Russia.  Business Insider
articles.full_text:
President Donald Trump's plan to buy potash from Belarus has drawn a warning from the leader of Canada's biggest potash-producing province, who says the fertilizer would have to be shipped through Russia.
His comments came after Trump said Monday that the US is negotiating a "massive Deal" to buy potash from Belarus.
"The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers.," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Potash is a key fertilizer ingredient used to boost crop yields, and Canada supplies the vast majority of US imports.
The proposal is the latest front in Trump's trade fight with Canada.
His administration has repeatedly targeted Canadian exports, although potash has largely been exempted from tariffs given its importance to US agriculture.
Scott Moe, the premier of Saskatchewan, argued that Belarusian potash would have to travel through Russia before reaching US farmers, raising questions about Trump's claim that it would be cheaper.
"Does anyone believe Belarusian blood potash shipped through Russia is going to be more affordable, more sustainable or more ethical than potash shipped from Saskatchewan - right here in North America?" Moe wrote in a post on X.
Belarus is landlocked, and sanctions imposed over its support for Russia's invasion of Ukraine, along with the loss of its main export route through Lithuania, have made its potash more expensive to ship to the US through Russia.
Moe has previously warned against using potash as a trade weapon.
As Canada weighed retaliatory trade measures last month, he urged Ottawa not to target potash exports, arguing that the move would hurt Canadian producers and encourage US buyers to look elsewhere.
Whether Belarus can significantly increase shipments to the US is also unclear.
Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko said earlier this month that Belarus had resumed selling potash to the US after Washington lifted sanctions on Belarusian potash producers.
He also called on Washington to release more than $40 million in Belarusian funds frozen in the US banking system.
On Monday, Lukashenko suggested Belarus may have little additional potash available for new Western buyers.
"We simply do not have those volumes - everything is contracted," he said, according to a post from his office.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: German foreign minister urges Russia to abandon dangerous escalation in rare meeting - The Guardian
articles.summary: Ukraine war briefing: German foreign minister urges Russia to abandon dangerous escalation in rare meeting  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
- 
  The foreign ministers of Russia and Germany met in New York on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, in the first such talks since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. But Russia’s top diplomat dismissed Germany’s calls to ease off its “dangerous path of escalation” toward Europe, instead accusing Germany of being Ukraine’s main sponsor and seeking to be a leading military power in Europe. “Does Berlin understand what this could lead to?” the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, asked in his speech at the gathering of world leaders on Saturday. “Didn’t they learn the lessons of world war two?”
- 
  German foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, used the talks to call on Russia “to abandon the dangerous path of escalation vis-a-vis Germany, Europe, and Nato”, according to a delegation source. Wadephul said incidents such as the attempted drone attack in Leipzig would not shake Germany’s resolve to support Ukraine, according to sources.
- 
  Relations between Moscow and Berlin have been frozen since the Russian invasion, and tensions escalated further after the drone incident at Leipzig airport. In a sign of the continued frostiness, Lavrov told a press conference on Saturday “nothing new” came from the talks with his German counterpart.
- 
  “I told him that frankly … you could just have called me and said: ‘read my statement’,” Lavrov said. “He simply reiterated his official public position condemning Russia … you can judge for yourself whether that counts as dialogue or not.”
- 
  Still, the ministers discussed bilateral ties and the war in Ukraine, officials from both sides said. Wadephul urged Lavrov to do “everything possible to reach an agreement on grain exports via the Black Sea”, a German delegation source said.
- 
  In a sign of the sensitivities around meeting the Russian foreign minister, Wadephul notified his European allies of the meeting afterwards in a message seen by Reuters. “I used this opportunity to reiterate our position on Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and to call for an immediate and complete ceasefire, most pressingly with a focus on grain exports, and the energy infrastructure,” he wrote.
- 
  After the meeting Lavrov addressed world leaders at the assembly, where he defended Russia’s war in Ukraine and lobbed barbs at the west — including Germany – and criticised the militarisation of Japan. He made clear that Russia will veto any attempt by Germany and Japan for permanent seats on the UN security council. The two nations fought Russia, Britain and the US in the second world war. Writing on her personal Telegram channel, Maria Zakharova, a spokesperson for Russia’s foreign ministry, said that “tens of diplomats” had come to meet Lavrov to “shake his hand and thank Russia”.
- 
  An overwhelming majority of general assembly member nations have repeatedly condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, as Wadephul noted in his own address to the assembly Saturday. “Russia’s war targets the lives of millions of innocent people, the existence of the Ukrainian state and culture and the European peace order,” he said, urging Russia to negotiating toward ending the fighting.
- 
  The talks came amid an intensifying aerial war and as Donald Trump said he hoped the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, would “settle” with Russia’s Vladimir Putin. With frontline positions largely unchanged since last year, Russia has hammered Ukraine with cruise and ballistic missiles, powerful glide bombs and jet-powered drones in recent months, while Ukraine’s long-range drones have targeted Russian oil refineries and businesses.
- 
  “It is essential that our partners not forget: Russia is escalating every single day,” Zelenskyy wrote on Saturday. “If the Russians have chosen to make their strikes even more brutal, the world must choose stronger responses to keep the war from spreading further.”
- 
  Ukrainian officials said Russian attacks killed four people on Saturday, as Russian authorities said a Ukrainian drone attack killed three.
- 
  Residents of Kyiv are preparing for power cuts, drone attacks and a bitter cold winter by stocking up on generators, food and “dry showers”, as the Ukrainian capital becomes a frontline city.
- 
  And Russia has opened a new front in its campaign against Ukraine, hitting several datacentres and internet providers in Kyiv this week in an apparent attempt to weaken the digital backbone of the economy.

- Zelenskyy's UN address: “Patient zero must be stopped”
	
- Deliberate strikes on evacuation hubs: the objective of human shields
	
- The siege of Oleshky: engineered famine and encirclement of 2,000 civilians in Kherson
	
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy leveraged the high-level debate of the 81st General Assembly of the United Nations (UN) to escalate diplomatic pressure on the international community, demanding a comprehensive global trade embargo against Moscow's energy revenues while highlighting the devastating human toll of the invasion, which has seen nearly 249,000 Russian casualties recorded in 2026 alone.
On the ground, however, kinetic warfare continues to intensify through systematic air strikes targeting civilian rescue convoys across the Donbas alongside the administrative starvation of occupied towns such as Oleshky. Operating from Kramatorsk, international correspondent María Senovilla delivers an operational assessment of the military and civilian crisis unfolding in eastern Ukraine.
Zelenskyy's UN address: “Patient zero must be stopped”
President Zelenskyy pursued an intensive diplomatic schedule at the United Nations, demanding additional integrated air defence capabilities and sovereign funding to halt the Russian advance.
His address before the UN General Assembly was exceptionally uncompromising. He urged international leaders to systematically sever the Kremlin's sovereign cash flows to prevent Vladimir Putin from sustaining his wartime military apparatus. He deployed a direct epidemiological metaphor: asserting that “patient zero must be stopped” to prevent the conflict from metastasising across neighbouring sovereign nations.
Zelenskyy stressed that any commercial trade channel channelling capital into Moscow directly subsidises military aggression against Ukraine, explicitly linking that strategic imperative to Ukraine's ongoing deep-strike campaign targeting commercial oil refineries deep within the Russian Federation: “We are directly burning down the Kremlin's sovereign revenues ourselves”.
He condemned the continued invocation of the veto power by Russia within the UN Security Council, designating it an institutional mechanism that actively paralyzes the rules-based international order. Putin did not attend the high-level summit in New York, constrained by the standing international arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC) for war crimes and the unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children.
The Ukrainian head of state presented stark military metrics regarding the war of attrition: across the first nine months of 2026, Russia sustained nearly 249,000 military personnel killed or wounded in action to secure barely one thousand square kilometres of territory.
Over that same operational timeframe, Ukrainian territory absorbed strikes from 63,000 Russian attack drones alongside more than 2,100 ballistic and cruise missiles, an operational volume significantly surpassing metrics recorded during the preceding year. There are no operational indicators suggesting Moscow intends to engage in durable ceasefire negotiations alongside NATO or European Union (EU) partners in the immediate term.
Deliberate strikes on evacuation hubs: the objective of human shields
Recent Russian precision strikes in Kramatorsk have specifically targeted designated civilian transit facilities and evacuation convoys. What operational objective is Moscow pursuing with these strikes?
Answer: Over recent days, extensive missile barrages have targeted Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa, but kinetic operations observed in Kramatorsk reveal a calculated tactical doctrine. Last Sunday, Russian precision strikes demolished the primary municipal civilian evacuation hub, located inside a school complex where classroom instruction has remained suspended since 2022.
These municipal facilities are routinely converted into logistical storage depots for humanitarian supplies, emergency power stations during grid blackouts, and temporary reception points for displaced families arriving from active frontline sectors including Kostiantynivka and Druzhkivka.
Kramatorsk has been officially reclassified as an active combat zone. Roughly 30,000 civilian residents remain out of an original pre-war population, while dedicated humanitarian emergency teams attempt to evacuate upwards of 500 individuals daily via protected transport vehicles heading toward the transit junction of Lozova or Western Ukraine.
I was reporting directly from that facility mere days ago, conducting interviews with families waiting for transit; barely 48 hours later, two Russian KAB precision-guided aerial bombs flattened the structure, causing severe civilian injuries. That no fatalities occurred was an extraordinary stroke of fortune.
Far from constituting accidental targeting errors, Russian combat aircraft struck the logistical operational headquarters of two accredited humanitarian organisations forty-eight hours later—Angels of Salvation and the Proliska mission—both tasked exclusively with non-combatant evacuation.
The Kremlin is actively executing a strategy to collapse civilian transit corridors, trapping the remaining non-combatant population within besieged municipal zones to exploit them as de facto human shields, thereby constricting the defensive fire doctrines of the Ukrainian armed forces.
The siege of Oleshky: engineered famine and encirclement of 2,000 civilians in Kherson
Across the southern operational theatre, acute humanitarian distress is documented in Oleshky, an occupied municipality located in the Kherson region.
We are observing an acute, engineered humanitarian disaster driven by a hermetic military encirclement. The Kherson oblast remains geographically bisected by the course of the Dnipro River: the northern bank is held by Ukrainian forces while the southern riverbank remains under Russian military occupation. Located within this southern sector is Oleshky, where Russian occupation forces have enforced a total operational blockade on commercial goods and humanitarian relief since May.
No food consignments, pharmaceutical supplies, or critical sanitary goods are permitted entry. Approximately 2,000 Ukrainian civilians—from a pre-invasion population of 24,000—survive under conditions of severe malnutrition. A verified field report published by the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (HRMMU) confirms that commercial stores remain shuttered, with running municipal water, gas networks, and electrical power entirely cut off. Trapped residents survive by foraging wild flora and searching abandoned residential properties for basic sustenance.
The tactical siege is reinforced by the dense mining of all secondary road corridors alongside armed drone interdiction operations targeting any civilians attempting to flee toward adjacent settlements. Civilians suffering from chronic medical conditions are dying systematically due to the total absence of essential pharmaceuticals.
While the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine has formally denounced this siege before United Nations human rights committees, official statements from the Kremlin dismiss documented violations as technical infrastructure interruptions, deliberately obfuscating a siege designed to starve trapped civilians.

articles.title: The War in the Middle East and Iran’s Bird’s-Eye View of the South Caucasus - Georgia Today
articles.summary: The War in the Middle East and Iran’s Bird’s-Eye View of the South Caucasus  Georgia Today
articles.full_text:
The war involving Iran is reshaping the strategic situation in the South Caucasus even though Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Georgia have remained outside the direct theater of hostilities. Its effects are nevertheless increasingly visible. The conflict is creating new security concerns, disrupting economic calculations, and accelerating geopolitical shifts that had already begun to transform the region before 2026.
The South Caucasus entered the current crisis at a particular moment when Russia’s traditional dominance had already been weakened by the war in Ukraine and by Moscow’s reduced ability to concentrate political, military, and economic resources on the region. Turkey, by contrast, had been steadily expanding its influence, particularly through its strategic relationship with Azerbaijan and its growing role in regional transport and trade. At the same time, East-West connectivity projects were gaining momentum as Europe and Central Asia sought alternatives to routes passing through Russia and Iran.
The result is a much more crowded geopolitical environment. The United States and the European Union have become more directly engaged in questions of regional peace, infrastructure, energy, and connectivity. China is seeking a larger economic and logistical role, while Central Asian states increasingly see the South Caucasus as their principal westward gateway. This has created a degree of geopolitical pluralism that is unusual for a region historically dominated by one or two major powers.
Iran occupies a distinctive position within this emerging order. Tehran has long regarded the South Caucasus as part of its immediate strategic neighborhood and as an area where developments can directly affect Iranian national security. It has never, however, been the dominant external power. Imperial Russia and later the Soviet Union shaped the regional order for much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, while the Russian Federation retained primacy after 1991.
Iran nevertheless played an important balancing role. It maintained close political and economic relations with Armenia, built significant trade ties with Azerbaijan despite recurrent political tensions, and preserved pragmatic relations with Georgia. More broadly, Tehran sought to prevent the South Caucasus from becoming a platform from which rival powers could project influence toward Iran itself. In Iranian strategic thinking, the deeper concern is the regional balance that infrastructure, alliances, and external security partnerships can eventually produce.
This is particularly evident in Iran’s approach to Armenia’s southern province of Syunik. For Tehran, the Armenian-Iranian border is a strategic asset that provides Iran with direct access to Armenia and, through Armenia and Georgia, to the Black Sea and potentially European markets. Any arrangement that could weaken Armenian control over Syunik has therefore been treated by Tehran with considerable suspicion.
This explains Iran’s longstanding hostility toward the idea of what Baku calls “Zangezur corridor” and its cautious, and often negative, response to the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity, or TRIPP. From Tehran’s perspective such a route becomes problematic if it is accompanied by new security arrangements or a reduction in Armenia’s effective sovereignty over the transit area.
The extent to which Iran regards this issue as strategic became visible in early March, when the US-Israeli military campaign began against Islamic Republic, and the latter struck the Nakhchivan exclave, through which the proposed route is expected to pass. The episode underlined an important feature of Iranian policy: connectivity is viewed as part of the regional balance of power.
At the same time, the war is weakening Iran’s ability to resist unfavorable regional developments through diplomacy, economic pressure, and political influence. Tehran must now devote greater attention and resources to immediate military and domestic priorities. This creates additional space for other actors to advance connectivity projects that Iran had previously attempted to slow, reshape, or balance.
This change coincides with the growth in Western-backed infrastructure initiatives. The United States, the European Union, Armenia, and Azerbaijan are increasingly linking regional normalization with transport development. In July, the European Union announced up to 200 million euros in grants for transport, energy, and digital infrastructure under its “Peace through Connectivity” initiative.
Washington has also expanded diplomatic and material support for TRIPP as railway and road projects connected to the broader regional transport network move forward. If these routes become operational, the South Caucasus could become more closely integrated into an East-West transport system connecting Central Asia, the Caspian Sea, Turkey, the Black Sea, and the European market, damaging Iran’s position.
Despite these profound changes, Tehran continues to perceive the region as an integrated strategic space linking Iran with Russia, the Black Sea, Europe, and Central Asia. Its objectives are largely defensive. Iran seeks to prevent the emergence of military or political arrangements that could threaten its northern borders.
This defensive logic also explains Iran’s prefrence for regional diplomatic mechanisms. Tehran has consistently supported the initiatives that bring together Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iran, Russia, and Turkey, with Georgia refusing to participate thus far. The approach reflects Iran’s broader conviction that the South Caucasus should be managed primarily by the states of the region rather than shaped by Western powers. For Tehran, the format serves several purposes. It limits the legitimacy of external involvement, keeps Iran institutionally involved in regional negotiations, and places it alongside Russia and Turkey despite the differences in their respective capabilities. Transit policy is another important part of this strategy. Iran wants the South Caucasus to remain connected to its own transport system rather than developing exclusively through East-West routes that bypass Iranian territory.
Therefore, the current war may therefore weaken Iran’s ability to shape events, but it does not necessarily change what Iran wants. Tehran will continue defending the Armenian-Iranian border, opposing the militarization of new corridors, promoting north-south connectivity, and resisting Western involvement.
Analysis by Emil Avdaliani*
*Emil Avdaliani is a research fellow at the Turan Research Center and a professor of international relations at the European University in Tbilisi, Georgia. His research focuses on the history of silk roads and the interests of great powers in the Middle East and the Caucasus.

articles.title: Armenia and Kazakhstan move to lessen their dependency on Russia - commonspace.eu
articles.summary: Armenia and Kazakhstan move to lessen their dependency on Russia  commonspace.eu
articles.full_text:
This analysis was prepared for commonspace.eu by Anna Szedlacsek, Deputy Editor and Junior Research Assistant at LINKS Europe.
Russia’s influence across the post-Soviet space has come under increasing pressure since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Two countries illustrate the changing relationship particularly clearly: Armenia, once one of Moscow’s closest military partners in the South Caucasus, and Kazakhstan, Russia’s largest and most strategically important partner in Central Asia.
Armenia and Kazakhstan both reached their strategic turning points between 2020 and 2022, driven by security failures, Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and severe economic vulnerabilities.
Among these reasons, the war in Ukraine sheds a particularly long shadow. In Kazakhstan, Russia’s “special military operation” substantially damaged Moscow's image among ordinary Kazakh citizens and reignited anxieties about revanchist Russian rhetoric regarding northern Kazakhstan. Public discontent has flared during Russian state visits and against Russian state projects like Rosatom’s nuclear power plant bid. Similarly, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, in 2022, in a bold statement at the 25th St. Petersburg International Economic Forum – sitting directly adjacent to Russian President Vladimir Putin – made it clear that Kazakhstan does not recognize Russia’s annexation of Ukrainian territories or the "quasi-states" in Donetsk and Luhansk. More recently, in July 2026, he also publicly called on Putin to reconsider his war policy, suggesting it was time to "freeze this conflict" and return to negotiations.
However, beyond the scope of diplomatic relations, Almaty is heavily challenged by having to navigate its deep economic and transit interdependence with Russia. Kazakhstan shares a 7,500 km land border with Russia and remains bound by shared membership in the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) and the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO). Crucially, over 80% of Kazakh crude oil exports cross Russian territory via the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) to Novorossiysk, giving Russia massive structural leverage.
To mitigate this reliance, Kazakhstan is aggressively developing alternative transport links, such as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (Middle Corridor) through Baku, Azerbaijan, to reach European and global markets without crossing Russian territory. This also reflects a move away from Russia as its main trading partner – this position has been earned by China, or, if considered as a bloc, the European Union (EU).
Armenia, on the other hand, began its pivot away from Moscow’s orbit after the 2020 Second Nagorno-Karabakh War and reached a point of no return following Azerbaijan's final capture of Nagorno-Karabakh in September 2023. This is due to the fact that despite hosting a Russian military base and belonging to the CSTO, Armenia received no military intervention from Russia during either of these conflicts. Moscow remained neutral – and thus turned untrustworthy in the eyes of Armenians – because it wished to safeguard its expanding economic, energy, and transit partnerships with Azerbaijan and Turkey. Concluding that Russia was no longer a reliable security guarantor and had its resources consumed by the war in Ukraine, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan suspended Armenia's participation in the CSTO in 2024 and began replacing Russian arms imports – which previously supplied over 90% of its arms – with defense systems from India and France. Furthermore, in March 2025, the Armenian parliament passed a law to initiate the EU accession process, while ministries are recruiting Western-educated professionals to restructure the civil service away from the Kremlin. Armenia has also concluded an energy cooperation agreement with Iran and is trying to strengthen its ties with China and India.
Ultimately, despite these developments, it would be premature to conclude the end of Moscow’s control over these countries, as both Armenia and Kazakhstan face severe structural constraints that strictly limit how far or how fast they can move away from Russia. Russia remains Armenia's primary trading partner, accounting for roughly 35% of its total foreign trade, and supplies 82% of the country’s natural gas at preferential prices via Gazprom, which owns Armenia's internal gas distribution network. Meanwhile, Almaty will certainly not dare risk a Russian halt along the CPC corridor as such a move would be detrimental to its state revenues and economy. It also continues to supply fuel to Russia during its refinery shortages and has just recently evaluated proposals to process Russian crude at Kazakh refineries.
The question, therefore, is not simply whether Russia is losing its allies. It is whether Russia is losing its ability to make those allies dependent on it.
As of September 2026, the evidence does not point to a definitive answer. Russia has not been pushed out of either country – but both Kazakhstan and Armenia appear increasingly eager to ensure that Moscow is no longer their only option.
This analysis was prepared for commonspace.eu by Anna Szedlacsek, Deputy Editor and Junior Research Assistant at LINKS Europe.

Why BlackRock Is Paying Attention
BlackRock Investment Institute's Ben Powell, who serves as chief investment strategist covering the Middle East and APAC, grouped Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan with the Gulf countries and India as places seeing more capital interest. In Kazakhstan specifically, he said the team is "very encouraged by the reform, the pension reform, the capital-market reform that we're seeing." Faster growth and policy shifts, plus rising demand for resources such as critical minerals, are helping put both economies on the map.
Kazakhstan's Draw: Flows, Reform and Oil Tailwinds
Through the start of the year, overseas investors have funneled about $2 billion into tenge‑denominated bonds. The country's output rose 4.1% from January through August, with manufacturing and construction doing much of the heavy lifting. Kazakhstan, the region's largest economy, sits between Russia and China and is lining up funding for a sizable infrastructure buildout, including a share offering by its railway operator and loans from the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank.
With oil trading higher, Central Asia's biggest energy exporter is getting an additional boost, owing to the US‑Israeli war with Iran sending Brent crude above $100 a barrel. "Kazakhstan becomes more friendly for capital, and when the country sees the benefits, it becomes even more friendly," Powell said. "If we see more opportunity, we would love to deploy more capital."

Russia will not halt its aggression against Ukraine even during possible negotiations, Russian Foreign Minister and the Kremlin’s highest-ranking representative Sergey Lavrov said during the United Nations (UN) Security Council meeting on Wednesday.
Russia rejected growing international calls for a ceasefire during a high-level Security Council meeting on Ukraine in New York, held at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
“Having learned from bitter experience, we will not pause the special military operation for the duration of negotiations in any format,” Kremlin’s highest-ranking representative said.
Ukraine would have kept its 1991 borders if the European nations had not “engaged in their shenanigans,” he continued, echoing Moscow’s long-standing hostility toward the West, just a month after Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day.
Sybiha: ‘Russia is vetoing peace’
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha condemned Lavrov’s comments during the same meeting on Wednesday.
“Fourteen of the 15 members of the UN Security Council support a ceasefire. Only one aggressor is blocking it,” Sybiha said, according to a statement from Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry.
The Security Council is the only UN body whose decisions can be legally binding on member states. The council has 15 members, including five permanent members: the US, UK, France, China and Russia.
Each permanent member can veto a substantive resolution, meaning Russia can block a resolution seeking to order action over the war it is waging against Ukraine.
Russia “illegally occupies the USSR’s seat at this table,” Sybiha said, calling for its removal from the Council.
He then addressed Lavrov directly, presenting three questions to Moscow; Why won’t Russian President Vladimir Putin meet President Volodymyr Zelensky? What did tens of thousands of Russian soldiers lost in August die for? And how, after four years after planning to take Kyiv in three days, is Moscow now burning?
Sybiha also urged members to demand humanitarian corridors for occupied Oleshky in the Kherson region. “If you remember only one thing from this meeting, remember Oleshky,” he said.
Oleshky, cut off from water, food and medicine, remains a humanitarian disaster as Russia failed to uphold the evacuation deal. Dmytro Lubinets, Ukrainian parliament commissioner for human rights, described the city as a “death trap,” with residents frequently risking being blown up by mines just to have a chance to escape through the woods.

articles.summary: Multiple trade routes help Iran evade sanctions  GIS Reports

Tehran’s economy is battered, yet parallel trade networks prevent its complete economic isolation.
GIS Radio
Listen to our AI-powered podcast for comprehensive insights.
- With Gulf access restricted, Iran uses costlier northern and eastern corridors
- Russia, China, Pakistan provide alternatives to Western-controlled routes
- Sanctions hurt Iran without delivering Washington’s desired outcome
- For comprehensive insights, tune into our AI-powered podcast here
To break the stalemate in its war with Iran, the administration of United States President Donald Trump is now trying to make Iran an international economic outcast with a new regime of sanctions. Iran has survived economic, military and diplomatic pressure from the U.S. and its allies since the 1979 Iranian revolution, albeit at great cost to its people.
This time, too, the Iranians expect to evade the most devastating impact of U.S. sanctions through the transportation and logistics networks they have created over the years to deal with Western pressure. Iran’s key partners in this effort so far have been Russia, Pakistan and China. This time around, Iran might also look to Turkiye as both a market and supplier, while expecting lukewarm implementation of sanctions or requests for exemptions from India.
The current war with Iran started because President Trump believed that his “maximum pressure” campaign against Iran was proving inadequate in preventing Tehran from developing nuclear weapons, neutralizing Iranian-backed terror networks and stopping the country’s missile armament.
The “Economic D-Day” announced by U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in August 2026 is an enhanced version of the February 2025 authorization the U.S. Treasury had to “impose maximum economic pressure” on the Iranian government.
Tehran circumventing sanctions
Before February 2025, Iran’s total trade stood at $110 billion annually. The sanctions limited Iran’s ability to sell its oil and to import commodities, yet China, Iraq and Turkiye remained Iran’s largest trading partners. Over the following year, China purchased 80-90 percent of Iran’s crude oil, worth nearly $32 billion. Trade with Iraq and Turkiye, both of which share land borders with Iran, was $10 billion and $5 billion, respectively.
The war that began on February 28, 2026, has disrupted Iran’s economy significantly, but there is no evidence that it has been completely crippled. Iran’s neighbors continue to serve as a lifeline, with cross-border commerce continuing in various forms, including illicit exchanges tolerated by border officials.
Among countries in Iran’s immediate neighborhood, the United Arab Emirates is the only one that has demonstrated the will to confront Iran, especially in the aftermath of Iran’s missile and drone attacks. Historically, the UAE was Iran’s second-largest trading partner, totaling $28 billion in 2024, for example. But the UAE implemented the U.S. “maximum pressure” sanctions and more recently, on August 19, 2026, suspended all trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran.
This meant that Iran lost all residual economic advantages of its historical business ties with the UAE, especially Dubai, where Iranian traders were once ubiquitous.
Limited by war and sanctions, Iran’s clerical regime, increasingly under control of the militant Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), understands that it can no longer depend on its Gulf ports as the main venue for its imports and exports. Tehran is now increasingly using its Caspian ports, including Bandar Anzali and Amirabad, and its land borders to manage continued economic activity.
Iran’s alternative trade routes
The Caspian corridor, free of disruption from the U.S. navy, allows Iran to maintain supplies of wheat, corn and edible oil, as well as military materials. But the Caspian ports have limited capacity and can only handle smaller vessels. Additionally, in July 2026, Ukraine targeted Iran-linked vessels in the Caspian Sea.
Using trucks to move goods through northern land routes is also much more expensive than shipping goods through ocean links. But in its effort to survive, Iran appears willing to pay that price for now; shipments across the Caspian Sea have reportedly increased significantly.
Iran-Pakistan trade and transport links
Iran and Pakistan share a relatively porous 900-kilometer border straddled by the ethnic Baloch people. Pakistan’s mediation role in the Iran war seems to have provided a boost to their trade and transport ties, which has, in turn, helped Iran evade Western sanctions.
Even before the latest war, Iran and Pakistan had tried to expand their economic and commercial partnership, in keeping with Pakistani leaders’ decades-old goal of regional economic integration with neighboring Muslim countries. Following President Trump implementing his maximum pressure sanctions, first in 2018 and reintroducing them in early 2025, Iran and Pakistan signed 12 agreements in August 2025, setting a target of $10 billion in bilateral trade by 2028.
Iranian-Pakistani commerce in March 2025 alone reached $3.13 billion. In its effort to circumvent sanctions, even this relatively small volume of trade was important for Iran, especially because cash payments and barter arrangements helped it bypass dollar-clearing requirements. Soon after mediating a ceasefire between Iran and the U.S. in June, Pakistan allowed the entry of goods originating from third countries into Iran overland through Pakistan.
When Iran attempted to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, Pakistan designated six road corridors linking its ports in Karachi, including Port Qasim, as well as in Gwadar, to the Gabd and Taftan land crossings through Balochistan for trade with Iran. These crossings have enabled exchanges in daily essentials as well as fuel, including electricity and gas.
The economy along the Iran-Pakistan land border operates with both formal customs procedures and smuggling of a wide range of goods, including liquified petroleum gas and other petroleum products, steel, food, agricultural goods and some manufactured items. Pakistan benefits by receiving cheap Iranian fuel and consumer goods, while Iranian suppliers are able to access Pakistan’s market and hard-currency transaction mechanisms.
Iran and Pakistan are currently implementing a barter mechanism and have applied the Customs Convention on the International Transport of Goods under Cover of TIR Carnets (TIR Convention, 1975), both of which enable them to bypass sanctions by avoiding the scrutiny in traditional banking channels. Pakistan often grants temporary exemptions from normal banking-instrument requirements for essential exports to Iran.
Iranians and Pakistanis seem to believe that the development of these overland routes has a long-term significance that will outlast the current war.
Husain Haqqani
Pakistan has also eased some export rules to facilitate transit trade between Iran and Central Asian countries through its territory. Islamabad has temporarily waived formal banking rules for essential supplies to Iran as well as Pakistani exports to Central Asian states, trying to bolster its own exports. As a consequence, Iran is building resilient transportation corridors through Pakistan and into Central Asia.
All of this ties in with Pakistan’s geostrategic ambitions. Islamabad has, for years, sought to make Pakistan a transit trade and energy corridor between the Middle East and Central Asia. Its leaders see an opportunity to attain that goal while the U.S. tries to bring the Iranian regime to heel through economic measures.
Iranians and Pakistanis seem to believe that the development of these overland routes has a long-term significance that will outlast the current war.
Iran and Russia
As two countries that are revisionist, revolutionary and seek to reprise their pride and status, Iran and Russia have a lot in common. Both Iran and Russia face Western sanctions and have built interdependence in financial, commercial and transportation fields.
Over time, Iran and Russia have moved to conduct bilateral financial settlements using a rial-ruble exchange bypassing the SWIFT architecture. Currently, 90 percent of their bilateral trade is through this mechanism linking Iran’s homegrown interbank telecommunication and financial messaging system SEPAM to Russia’s alternative to SWIFT, called SPFS. Even though bilateral trade stands at only $5 billion, it avoids Western sanctions and banking restrictions.
Given its geography, regional influence and strategic interests, Russia has been key to Iran’s attempts to build resilient and efficient supply chains. The 2025 Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty between the two countries institutionalized what has been built over the previous two decades.
The central element of this effort is the International North-South Transit Corridor (INSTC), which was established in 2000 by India, Russia and Iran as an alternative transportation corridor and trade route to the Suez Canal. Currently, 75 percent of the entire project has been completed. According to the Kazakhstan-based Eurasian Development Bank, the corridor will be able to haul 30 million tons by 2030, providing $1.5 billion in transit fees to Iran.

The next step of the project involves completion of the Rasht-Astara railway, which would give unimpeded railway access from St. Petersburg in Russia to Bandar-Abbas in Iran.

Updates to Russia/Belarus sanctions from EU and UK (and major US developments)
With the rapid expansion of UK, EU and US sanctions on Russia and Belarus in recent weeks - and with more in the regulatory pipeline - we set out:
If you would like to discuss any sanctions-related issues with a specialist, please contact Partner Andrew Hood, who would be pleased to arrange an initial conversation about your query: Andrew.Hood@fieldfisher.com or +44 330 460 6968.
1. WHAT'S NEW
Key sanctions developments from the UK, EU and US from September 2026.
i. UK
- On 14 September 2026, the Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI) added FAQ 203 on crediting interest to frozen accounts of designated persons. FAQ 203 clarifies that interest may be credited only to the frozen account in which it accrues, and not to another frozen account even if it is held by the same designated person. OFSI reminds firms to consider whether a licence is required before making such payments.
ii. EU
- On 21 September 2026, European Commission Vice President, Kaja Kallas, confirmed that the EU will impose new sanctions on those involved in organising the Russian State Duma elections held between 18 – 20 September 2026. Her statement notes that "those involved in organising these sham elections or standing as candidates in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, as well as those responsible for undermining the possibility of free and fair elections inside Russia, will be sanctioned". Further details of the proposed sanctions have not yet been announced.
- On 16 September 2026, European Commission President, Ursula von der Leyen, made her State of the Union speech sharing her key priorities and strategic direction for the year to come. In relation to Russia sanctions, von der Leyen stated that "the pressure on Russia must continue to increase…and this does not always require new sanctions, but above all the enforcement of existing ones". The speech made no indication of when the European Commission is set to deliver the 22nd EU sanctions package.
- On 14 September 2026, the EU failed to extend its asset freeze regulation following a demand from Slovakia that the EU remove Alisher Usmanov and Michail Fridman from the list. France has reportedly attempted to create a compromise by suggesting that Alisher Usmanov be delisted. Member States agreed on a one-week extension to allow negotiations to continue on the six-monthly rollover of the sanctions, which requires the unanimous approval of the 27 Member States.
- On 12 September 2026, Advocate General Medina (the "AG") issued a non-binding opinion on the scope of Article 5k of Regulation (EU) 833/2014. The AG's view is that the Article 5k prohibition on certain Russian nationals and companies being awarded public procurement contracts only applies where a contract is in scope of the EU public procurement framework, including the EU's threshold amounts. Member States cannot expand the scope of the Article even if their domestic legislation applies procurement rules to lower-value contracts.
iii. US
- On 16 September 2026, the United States House passed the H.R.5334 Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. For more detail, please refer to: The New US Sanctioning Russia Act: Considerations for Businesses. 
2. YOUR 5-STEP CHECKLIST
Working through the following 5 questions will help you to better manage your business's sanctions compliance:
We step through the key considerations that will help you answer each question below.
- Which countries’ sanctions apply to your activities?
The UK, EU, US and other countries’ sanctions typically must be observed if there is a sufficient nexus to confer jurisdiction, that is if:
- their nationals (individuals) are involved, wherever they are in the world (in the case of US sanctions, this includes US permanent residents/Green Card holders);
- any part of a transaction is conducted within their territory or airspace; and
- legal entities incorporated or constituted under their law, including foreign branches are involved; or
- with respect to US sanctions, if a transaction is conducted in US dollars or clears through the US financial system, or data is routed through servers in the US, or other back-office support or facilitation is provided by US persons (including service requests to an equipment supplier). Non-US persons may be penalised if they cause US persons to violate US sanctions, for example omitting reference to the involvement of a sanctioned party or jurisdiction to a financial transaction involving a US person.
UK sanctions may also apply to non-UK persons outside the UK if there is a sufficient nexus. This will depend on the facts of each case but could include:
- transactions using clearing services in the UK;
- actions by a local subsidiary of a UK company;
- actions directed from within the UK; and/or
- financial products or insurance bought on UK markets but held or used overseas.
Additionally, US ‘secondary sanctions’ may be applied to non-US persons outside the US in the absence of any US nexus if a transaction involves sanctionable conduct that would be prohibited to a US person and that is determined by the US authorities to be a ‘significant’ transaction or otherwise provides material support to a sanctioned party. Whether a transaction is ‘significant’ is based on a number of open-ended criteria e.g. the size, number and frequency of transactions.
Further, US export control restrictions may apply even if sanctions do not. For example, US export controls will apply if US-origin goods, software or technology located in a third country are re-exported, regardless of whether a U.S. person is involved in the transaction.
- Are any of your business partners (banks, suppliers, customers, distributors etc.) subject to an asset freeze?
The UK, EU, US and others have imposed asset freezes (‘blocking sanctions’ in US terms) on most Russian banks, individuals and entities involved in strategic industries (e.g. defence, energy, finance, transport, research, media and aerospace), and senior individuals in the Russian government, state-owned corporations and major businesses, including family members, and they are continuing to add new names to their national lists of such ‘designated persons’. As the various sanctions regimes have matured, asset freezes have increasingly been imposed on third country entities and individuals (including those based in China, Turkey, the UAE etc.).
An asset freeze generally requires those within the scope of the national sanctions, as described at step 1 (above), to:
- freeze any assets of the designated parties that they may hold and to report these to their authorities;
- not make any funds or economic resources available to them, directly, indirectly or for their benefit (economic resources are broadly defined).
US and some EU restrictions go further and prohibit all transactions with the designated (i.e. listed) party.
The same restrictions also apply to any non-designated entity that is:
- ‘owned’ by a designated party or parties. The US and EU threshold is 50% or more, while the UK threshold is ‘more than 50%’. The US and the EU (in guidance) consider the criterion met if the aggregated ownership of two or more designated parties exceeds the threshold. The UK recognises aggregated ownership only if there is evidence of a joint arrangement between two or more designated parties; or
- (in the UK/EU, not the US) ‘controlled’ by a designated entity (i.e. able to ensure the affairs of the undesignated entity are conducted in accordance with their wishes, for example through controlling a majority of voting shares or having the right to appoint or remove a majority of the board of directors).
'Control' considerations:
It is often challenging to reach a definitive view of whether this ‘control’ criterion is applicable, for example if a majority shareholder becomes sanctioned and passes some of their shares to unsanctioned family members or to business associates. Some key considerations are set out below:
UK: The UK courts and Government have all contributed to a somewhat uncertain definition of 'control'.
The Court of Appeal's 2023 judgment in Boris Mints & Ors v PJSC National Bank Trust (NBT) & Anor implies that all Russian state-owned companies may be controlled by President Putin, a designated person. The judgement is being appealed to the Supreme Court.
The UK High Court's judgment in Hellard v OJSC Rossiysky Kredit Bank & Ors discusses the test for "control" in light of the Mints judgment, breaking the concept of control into 4 categories: de jure control; actual present de facto control; potential future de jure control and potential future de facto control.
UK Government guidance published after the ruling in Mints states that: "If [Government] considered that a public official was exercising control over the public body under UK sanctions regulations, [the Government] would look to designate the public body where possible when designating the relevant public official." That is, in the view of the UK Government, simply being run or overseen by a UK designated public official would not of itself mean the organisation is subject to UK sanctions.
The 2025 High Court judgment in Nikolay Fetisov & Ilya Yurov & PJSC National Bank Trust applied the above judgments when considering whether President Putin and/or Central Bank of the Russian Federation Governor Elvira Nabiullina "control" NBT (the same entity considered in the Mints decision. In this case, the Court found that the absence of evidence of potential de facto control was significant, ultimately deciding that NBT was not "controlled" by a designated person and therefore did not need to be treated as subject to an asset freeze. This aligned with a statement from OFSI presented in evidence noting that "OFSI does not consider NBT to be subject to sanctions."

articles.summary: U.S. Pushes To Turn Armenia-Azerbaijan Transit Deal Into Investment Opportunity  Ազատություն Ռադիոկայան
articles.full_text:
Senior regional officials and executives from more than 40 companies gathered in New York on September 23 to discuss the next steps for the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), a centerpiece of Washington's efforts to turn the Armenia-Azerbaijan opening into greater regional trade and investment.
The event, held on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, featured US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Republican Senator Steve Daines of Montana, as well as officials from Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and the five Central Asian states.
The challenge now is turning a political agreement into steel, asphalt and investment. No construction has begun, feasibility studies are still underway, and companies are not expected to begin competing for major contracts until late 2026 or early 2027. Washington envisions TRIPP as a multimodal corridor through southern Armenia linking Azerbaijan with its Nakhchivan exclave while creating a wider east-west connection between the South Caucasus, Central Asia and Western markets.
The proposed Armenian section is only about 43 kilometers long, but it seeks to resolve one of the most contentious issues to emerge from decades of conflict between Armenia and Azerbaijan: how to connect mainland Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenian territory.
Armenia and Azerbaijan fought two major wars over Nagorno-Karabakh, an internationally recognized part of Azerbaijan that for decades had a predominantly ethnic-Armenian population. Azerbaijan regained full control of the territory in 2023, prompting almost all of its ethnic-Armenian population to flee.
The two countries agreed on the text of a peace treaty in March 2025 but have yet to complete a final agreement. At a White House summit five months later, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed a U.S.-brokered joint declaration aimed at ending decades of conflict and opening regional transport links. TRIPP emerged from that agreement.
TRIPP is intended to provide unimpeded transit between mainland Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan through Armenian territory while preserving Armenia's sovereignty, territorial integrity and jurisdiction -- a politically important provision given long-running disputes over control of the route.
The project would be developed by a U.S.-Armenian company in which the United States would have a controlling stake, giving Washington a significant role in a strategically important region where Russia has traditionally wielded considerable influence. Under the plan, the Armenian section would eventually carry rail and road links as well as energy and digital infrastructure. Witkoff credited Pashinian and Aliyev with recognizing that a peace agreement offered a better alternative to decades of conflict.
“Unlike many other conflicts that we see in the world, we had all the ingredients of a deal here,” Witkoff said, describing the two leaders as “incredibly pragmatic and mature.”
He also credited Trump with pushing the process forward after US officials found communication between Yerevan and Baku had stalled. The focus in New York, however, was on whether the diplomatic opening can now produce economic benefits. Witkoff said the economic implications of TRIPP had become increasingly apparent as officials and companies examined its potential role in international supply chains.
“Everybody's focused now on transmission and speed to market,” he said, citing estimates that the route could cut some trade journeys by up to three weeks.
TRIPP could feed into the wider Trans-Caspian, or Middle Corridor, an east-west network carrying goods between China and Central Asia through the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus and onward to Europe. The route has attracted increased attention as governments and businesses seek alternatives to traditional transit routes through Russia. Witkoff said he expected the project to generate “huge investment,” particularly in Armenia.
Speaking separately in New York on September 23, Pashinian said implementation of TRIPP would “fully unlock” regional connectivity and “open a new era” for Armenia and its economy. For now, however, the corridor remains largely on paper.
The State Department says engineering and feasibility studies are examining the proposed railway route, including technical, environmental and social considerations. A separate pre-feasibility study is looking at placing energy and digital infrastructure alongside transportation links.
Officials expect the railway feasibility work to be completed by late 2026 or early 2027, after which companies could bid for contracts. Construction of the railway would take at least another 18 months, while electricity connections could potentially begin operating in 2027. Washington is also building financial and corporate structures intended to turn those plans into investable projects.
The United States and Armenia are establishing a TRIPP Development Company, a joint venture in which Washington is expected to hold a majority stake and which would oversee infrastructure development and competitive tenders. A separate Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund is intended to mobilize private capital for connectivity projects across the wider region.
Andrew D'Anieri, associate director of the Atlantic Council's Eurasia Center, said the two initiatives signaled deeper U.S. economic engagement.
“Advancing TRIPP and announcing the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund in the presence of senior regional officials and major U.S. companies sends a strong signal that America means business,” D'Anieri told RFE/RL.
“TRIPP will advance more slowly given the degree of technical project difficulty and geopolitical sensitivities,” he said.
Those sensitivities extend well beyond Armenia and Azerbaijan. The South Caucasus connects Europe with Central Asia in a region where Russia, China, Iran and Turkey all have significant interests.
Angela Howard, a research analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies' Center on Economic and Financial Power, said U.S.-backed infrastructure could create new trade links while reducing dependence on Russian-controlled or influenced routes.
“U.S. investment in the Caucasus places an American foot in the gateway to Central Asia,” she told RFE/RL.
She cautioned, however, that US-backed projects would require safeguards against corruption and foreign influence.
“Strong guardrails and extensive oversight will be critical moving forward,” Howard said.
Daines said Washington needed to sustain its engagement and argued that the region should be viewed not only through the lens of past conflicts but also as a potential hub for trade and investment.
For now, the political framework exists, but engineering studies, financing, tenders and construction still lie ahead. As one senior US official put it, “We are not at that stage yet.”
